source_refs.note: Topic 5.9, printed pages 106-107 (Figure 5.9). The print's 'Table (5.9)' is Table 5.4.

blocks.text: When a liquid is heated its vapour pressure keeps increasing, and a stage is reached when the vapour pressure equals the atmospheric or external pressure; at this temperature the liquid starts boiling. The bubbles of vapour formed in the interior of the liquid now have a greater internal pressure than the atmospheric pressure on the surface, so they rise out of the liquid and burst at the surface, and a constant stream of bubbles comes out at the boiling point. Heating a liquid raises the kinetic energy of its molecules and so its temperature; at the boiling point the kinetic energy is at its maximum, and further heating does not raise the temperature but is used to break the intermolecular forces and convert the liquid into vapour. Figure 5.9 shows the vapour pressures of water, ethyl alcohol, ethylene glycol and diethyl ether against temperature: each liquid reaches its boiling point when its vapour pressure equals 760 torr at sea level, diethyl ether at 34.6, ethanol at 78.3 and water at 100 degrees C.

blocks.alt: A graph of vapour pressure (0 to 800 torr) against temperature (0 to 120 degrees C) for four liquids. Each curve rises steeply. Diethyl ether reaches 760 torr, and boils, at 34.6 C, ethanol at 78.3 C and water at 100 C; ethylene glycol's curve stays near the axis because it boils far above 100 C.
blocks.caption: Vapour pressures (torr) of four common liquids against temperature (original diagram after Figure 5.9).
